approved: Home Affairs Legislation Amendment (2025 Measures No. 1) Bill 2025
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill would confirm the lawfulness of past and future government actions concerning offshore processing and certain visa refusals.
It would amend the Migration Act 1958 to remove the requirement for procedural fairness when the government makes deals with foreign countries on third country reception arrangements.
It would also validate visa decisions that were overturned by a court because the minister relied on a now-overruled High Court ruling about indefinite detention.
The bill would make the rules of natural justice inapplicable to entering or preparing third country reception arrangements with foreign countries.
It would validate any past actions taken in relation to those arrangements that were invalid only because natural justice was not observed.
It would validate certain protection visa refusal decisions that were set aside by the Full Federal Court in the AJN23 case.
non-citizens subject to removal pathway arrangements, and protection visa applicants whose decisions were influenced by the now-overruled Al-Kateb ruling

Home Affairs Legislation Amendment (2025 Measures No. 1) Bill 2025 - Limitation of Debate - Pass the bill

Announced that, unless otherwise ordered, the Home Affairs Legislation Amendment (2025 Measures No.1) Bill 2025 would stand referred to the Federation Chamber if consideration had not concluded before question time.

Moved that the Legal and Constitutional Affairs Legislation Committee hold a public hearing at 5 pm on 3 September 2025, for not less than two hours, to hear Home Affairs officials about the Home Affairs Legislation Amendment (2025 Measures No. 1) Bill 2025; the question was agreed to.

Moved that standing order 111 paragraphs (5) to (8) not apply to the Home Affairs Legislation Amendment (2025 Measures No. 1) Bill 2025, allowing consideration during the period of sittings; the question was agreed to.

Reported that two votes deferred from the previous evening, together with a vote on the Home Affairs Legislation Amendment (2025 Measures No. 1) Bill 2025, could be dealt with. The Senate then considered a motion concerning restoration of a bill to the Notice Paper and referral to the Legal and Constitutional Affairs Legislation Committee.

Reported a deferred vote on a closure motion concerning whether the Home Affairs Legislation Amendment (2025 Measures No. 1) Bill 2025 should proceed without formality, then moved that the bill be read a first time.
Moved that questions on remaining stages of four bills be put at 1 pm on 4 September 2025, with debate limited and divisions permitted between 1.30 pm and 2 pm; the motion was agreed to.

Moved to suspend standing orders to expedite consideration of the Home Affairs Legislation Amendment (2025 Measures No. 1) Bill 2025, arguing that it removes natural justice for asylum seekers and others facing deportation to Nauru, lacks urgency, restricts scrutiny, and targets multicultural communities; cited evidence that the Nauru arrangement could be a $2.5 billion deal.

Supported the Home Affairs Legislation Amendment (2025 Measures No. 1) Bill 2025 as necessary to strengthen the removal framework and address procedural fairness, while arguing that it did not ensure community safety; cited 354 members of the NZYQ cohort and said the Nauru arrangement could cost more than $2.5 billion over 30 years, urging preventive detention and stronger mandatory-detention provisions.
